doc_summary: Hubinger argues that current models are fairly well aligned but that the hard parts of alignment (scalable oversight, hard-to-detect misaligned personas, long-horizon RL) are not yet encountered, because present misalignment is easy to detect and verify. He lays out research priorities such as interpretability, model organisms, and evaluating on real high-stakes distributions.

items.claim: Prefers treating current easily-detected misbehaviour (reward hacking, agentic misalignment) as the easy version of alignment over treating it as evidence that alignment is solved, because it is overt, visible in chain-of-thought, and elicitable by fake scenarios, and so says little about future models that hide misalignment.
items.quote: all of the cases where we’ve inadvertently selected for misaligned personas—alignment faking, agentic misalignment, etc.—are cases where the misaligned personas are easy to detect: they put the misaligned reasoning directly in their chain-of-thought, they’re overtly misaligned rather than hiding it well, and we can generate fake scenarios that elicit their misalignment.

items.claim: Distrusts behavioral evaluations as models become more capable, since models get better at telling when they are in evaluations and at acting aligned within them.
items.quote: we already see personas that try to hide their misalignment, they’re just not very good at it right now—but we are already seeing signs that models are getting better at telling when they’re in evaluations

items.claim: In a setup, evaluate on real high-stakes distributions such as actual internal usage data instead of synthetic scenarios, because the closer the eval is to the deployment distribution, the harder it is for models to detect it and behave differently.
items.quote: One additional thing I would put under this category also is evaluating models on the actual real high-stakes distributions of interest—e.g. real internal usage data of researchers at labs using models for AI research.

items.claim: Expects that even on-distribution evals will eventually be detectable, because they are necessarily built from past data, which differs systematically from future data.
items.quote: While eventually models will likely be able to detect even such evaluations (because they are still by necessity be based on past data, which is systematically different than future data)

items.claim: Reads over-the-top behaviours like blackmail as signs of a crude, fiction-derived persona and so of an eval/scenario-driven artifact, not of sophisticated misalignment, which suggests that more subtle and realistic scenarios are needed to probe capable personas.
items.quote: the sort of over-the-top stuff like blackmail is I think clearly coming from (2)-adjacent sources—but as models get more capable, I think we’re likely to see more personas like (4), which are much scarier and could be much better at hiding misalignment.

items.claim: Prefers cognitive (white-box/interpretability) oversight over purely behavioral oversight because behavioral evidence degrades as models get better at acting aligned in evaluations, while internal signals have no similar fundamental reason to degrade.
items.quote: a more capable model can do a better job of acting aligned in evaluations, but not clearly a better job of not thinking about that when doing so.

items.claim: Prefers model organisms where misalignment is constructed to be evaluable over studying natural cases, because they give a ground-truth testbed for iterating on hard problems that can't yet be observed in the wild.
items.quote: they give us a testing ground for iteration in which we know how to evaluate alignment (because the misalignment is constructed to be evaluable), from which we can then generalize to the real case where we don’t think we can reliably evaluate alignment.

items.claim: Chooses what to test by looking at where training is heading, such as long-horizon tasks that select for resource acquisition and self-preservation, and studies those with model organisms before they appear in practice.
items.quote: the next big thing I want to focus on here is the long-horizon RL problem, which I think is just at the point where we can likely study it with model organisms, even if we’re not yet encountering it in practice.

items.claim: Treats model-organism work as valuable partly as persuasive evidence that hard problems are real, not only for the technical lessons.
items.quote: even when we don’t learn direct lessons about how to solve the hard problems of alignment, this work is critical for producing the evidence that the hard problems are real, which is important for convincing the rest of the world to invest substantially here.

items.claim: Holds that behaving well in checkable situations is insufficient evidence; what matters is whether models behave well for the right reasons so that good behaviour generalizes to unchecked situations.
items.quote: rather than just ensuring models behave well in situations we can check, inner alignment is the problem of ensuring that they behave well *for the right reasons* such that we can be confident they will generalize well in situations we can’t check.
